nodes.name: Radical of an integer
nodes.statement: Associated to any non-zero integer $n$ is its radical \begin{align*} \rad(n)=\prod_{p\mid n}p. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The radical rad(n) is the product of the distinct primes dividing n.

nodes.name: abc triple of exponent lambda
nodes.statement: We say that a triple $(a,b,c)\in \N^3$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ is an $abc$ \emph{triple of exponent} $\lambda$ if \begin{align*} a+b=c,\quad \rad(abc) < c^{\lambda}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A coprime triple with a+b=c and rad(abc) < c^lambda.

nodes.name: abc conjecture
nodes.statement: The well-known $abc$ conjecture of Masser and Oesterl\'e asserts that, for any $\lambda<1$, there are only finitely many $abc$ triples of exponent $\lambda$.
conclusions: there are only finitely many $abc$ triples of exponent $\lambda$

nodes.name: Stewart-Yu theorem on the abc conjecture
nodes.statement: The best unconditional result is due to Stewart and Yu~\cite{styu}, who have shown that finitely many $abc$ triples satisfy $\rad(abc) < (\log c)^{3-\eps}$.

nodes.name: Counting function N_lambda(X)
nodes.statement: {} For $\lambda>0$ define $N_\lambda(X)$ as the number of triples $(a,b,c)\in \N^3$ with $a+b=c$, $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ and $\rad(abc) < c^{\lambda}$.
nodes.statement_short: N_lambda(X) counts coprime triples a+b=c with rad(abc) < c^lambda.
nodes.label: def:Nlambda

nodes.name: de Bruijn radical bound
nodes.statement: For any $\ve>0$, we have \begin{equation} \#\left\{n\leq x : \rad(n)\leq x^\lambda\right\} \ll_\ve x^{\lambda+\ve}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Integers up to x with radical at most x^lambda number at most x^(lambda+eps).
nodes.label: lem:deBruijnRadical

nodes.name: Equation (1.1)
nodes.statement: \#\left\{n\leq x : \rad(n)\leq x^\lambda\right\} \ll_\ve x^{\lambda+\ve}.
nodes.label: eq:bruijn

nodes.name: Proof of de Bruijn radical bound
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that for any integer $k\geq 2$ we have \begin{align} |\{n\leq X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}|\ll X^{O(1/\log \log X)}. \end{align} To prove \eqref{eq1}, write $k=p_1\cdots p_r$ as distinct primes $p_1<\cdots <p_r$. Then $\rad(n)=k$ implies that $n=p_1^{m_1}\cdots p_{r}^{m_r}$ for some integers $m_1,\ldots, m_r\geq 1$. Therefore, the number of $n\leq X$ in question is \begin{align*} |\{n\leq X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}| &\leq \sum_{m_1,\ldots, m_r\geq 1}\1_{\sum_{j\leq r}m_j(\log p_j)\leq \log X}\\ &\leq \sum_{m_1,\ldots, m_r\geq 1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^r}\1_{\sum_{j\leq r}t_j(\log p_j)\leq \log X}\1_{t_j\in (m_j-1,m_j]\, \forall j\leq r} \d t_1\cdots \d t_r\\ &=\textnormal{vol}\Big(\big\{(t_1,\ldots, t_r)\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^r:\,\, t_1(\log p_1)+\cdots +t_r(\log p_r)\leq \log X\big\}\Big)\\ &=(\log X)^re^{O(r)}r^{-r}\prod_{j=1}^r \frac{1}{\log p_j} \end{align*} by calculating the volume of a simplex. Moreover, we have \begin{align*} \prod_{j=1}^r \log p_j\geq \prod_{j=2}^{r+1}\log j=\exp\left(\sum_{j=2}^{r+1}\log \log j\right)\gg (\log r)^{r}e^{-O(r)}. \end{align*} Hence for some $C_0>1$ \begin{align*} |\{n\leq X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}| \ll \left(\frac{C_0\log X}{r\log r}\right)^r\ll \exp\Big(O\Big(\frac{\log X}{\log\log X}\Big)\Big), \end{align*} since $r=\omega(k)\leq (1+o(1))(\log X)/(\log \log X)$ by the prime number theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to counting n with fixed radical k; bound this by the volume of a simplex, then use the prime number theorem for omega(k).

nodes.name: Equation (1.2)
nodes.statement: |\{n\leq X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}|\ll X^{O(1/\log \log X)}.
nodes.label: eq1

nodes.statement: It suffices to show that for any integer $k\geq 2$ we have \begin{align} |\{n\leq X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}|\ll X^{O(1/\log \log X)}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to bounding the number of n with radical k.

nodes.name: Lower-bound the product of log p_j
nodes.statement: Moreover, we have \begin{align*} \prod_{j=1}^r \log p_j\geq \prod_{j=2}^{r+1}\log j=\exp\left(\sum_{j=2}^{r+1}\log \log j\right)\gg (\log r)^{r}e^{-O(r)}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Combine and use the prime number theorem bound on omega(k)
nodes.statement: Hence for some $C_0>1$ \begin{align*} |\{n\leq X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}| \ll \left(\frac{C_0\log X}{r\log r}\right)^r\ll \exp\Big(O\Big(\frac{\log X}{\log\log X}\Big)\Big), \end{align*} since $r=\omega(k)\leq (1+o(1))(\log X)/(\log \log X)$ by the prime number theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Combine and use the prime number theorem bound on omega(k).

nodes.name: Trivial bound for N_lambda
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda>0$. Then $N_\lambda(X)=O_\ve( X^{2\lambda/3+\ve})$, for any $\ve>0$.
nodes.label: prop:ABCTrivialBound

nodes.name: Proof of trivial bound for N_lambda
nodes.statement: Any triple $(a,b,c)$ counted by $N_\lambda(X)$ must satisfy $\rad(abc)< X^{\lambda}$, and so we must have $\min\{\rad(a)\rad(b),\rad(b)\rad(c),\rad(c)\rad(a)\}< X^{2\lambda/3}$, since $a,b,c$ are pairwise coprime. An application of~\ref{lem:deBruijnRadical} now leads to the following ``trivial bound''.
nodes.statement_short: Pairwise coprimality gives a pair with small radical product; apply de Bruijn's bound.
also_stated_at: Any triple $(a,b,c)$ counted by $N_\lambda(X)$ must satisfy $\rad(abc)< X^{\lambda}$, and so we must have $\min\{\rad(a)\rad(b),\rad(b)\rad(c),\rad(c)\rad(a)\}< X^{2\lambda/3}$, since $a,b,c$ are pairwise coprime. An application of~\eqref{eq:bruijn} now leads to the following ``trivial bound''.

nodes.name: Exceptional abc triple bound
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda\in (0, 1.001)$ be fixed. Then $N_\lambda(X)=O( X^{33/50})$.
nodes.statement_short: For lambda < 1.001, the number of abc triples of exponent lambda up to X is O(X^{0.66}).
nodes.label: thm:ABCExceptionalBound

nodes.name: Comparison with the trivial bound
nodes.statement: Here we note that $33/50=0.66$. By comparison, the trivial bound in Proposition~\ref{prop:ABCTrivialBound} would give $N_1(X)=O(X^{0.66\bar{6}+\eps})$ and $N_{1.001}(X)=O(X^{0.6674})$. Moreover, we see that Theorem~\ref{thm:ABCExceptionalBound} gives a power-saving when $\lambda\in (0.99,1.001)$.
nodes.statement_short: The main bound beats the trivial bound X^{2lambda/3} when lambda is in (0.99,1.001).

nodes.name: Mazur's question on N_lambda
nodes.statement: Given a fixed $\lambda>1$, he asked whether or not $ N_\lambda(X)$ has exact order $ X^{\lambda-1}$.

nodes.name: Refined counting function S_{alpha,beta,gamma}(X)
nodes.statement: For $\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0$, define $S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$ as the number of $(a,b,c)\in \N^3$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ such that \[ a,b,c\in [1,X], \quad a+b=c, \quad \rad(a)\leq X^\alpha, \quad \rad(b)\leq X^\beta, \quad \rad(c)\leq X^\gamma. \]
nodes.statement_short: S counts coprime triples in [1,X] with a+b=c and radicals of a,b,c bounded by X^alpha, X^beta, X^gamma.
nodes.label: def:Sabc

nodes.name: Trivial bound for S_{alpha,beta,gamma}
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll_\ve X^{\min\{\alpha+\beta , \alpha+\gamma , \beta+\gamma\}+\ve}, \end{equation} for any $\ve>0$.
nodes.label: lem:TrivialBdforS

nodes.name: Equation (1.3)
nodes.statement: S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll_\ve X^{\min\{\alpha+\beta , \alpha+\gamma , \beta+\gamma\}+\ve},
nodes.label: eq:trivial

nodes.name: Mazur's question on S_{alpha,beta,gamma}
nodes.statement: Mazur then asks whether $S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$ has order $X^{\alpha+\beta+\gamma-1}$ if $\alpha+\beta+\gamma>1$.

nodes.name: Kane's bounds for S_{alpha,beta,gamma}
nodes.statement: Evidence towards this has been provided by Kane~\cite[Theorems~1 and 2]{kane}, who proves that \[ X^{\alpha+\beta+\gamma-1-\ve}\ll_\ve S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll_\ve X^{\alpha+\beta+\gamma-1+\ve}+X^{1+\ve}, \] for any $\ve>0$, provided that $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in (0,1]$ are fixed and satisfy $\alpha+\beta+\gamma>1$.
nodes.statement_short: Kane: S is between X^{alpha+beta+gamma-1-eps} and X^{alpha+beta+gamma-1+eps}+X^{1+eps}.

nodes.name: Darmon-Granville finiteness theorem
nodes.statement: For example, it follows from work of Darmon and Granville~\cite{DG} that there are only finitely many coprime integer solutions to the Diophantine equation $x^p+y^q=z^r$, when $p,q,r\in \mathbb{N}$ are given and satisfy $1/p+1/q+1/r<1$.
conclusions: there are only finitely many coprime integer solutions to the Diophantine equation $x^p+y^q=z^r$

nodes.name: Proof outline of the exceptional abc triple bound
nodes.statement: We now describe the main ideas behind the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:ABCExceptionalBound}. In terms of the counting function $S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$, our task is to show that whenever $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in (0,1]$ satisfy $\alpha+\beta+\gamma\leq \lambda$, we have $ S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll X^{2\lambda/3-\eta}, $ for some $\eta>0$. A simple factorisation lemma (Proposition~\ref{prop:DiophantineReduction}) will reduce the problem of bounding $S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$ to the problem of bounding the number of solutions to various Diophantine equations of the shape \[ \prod_{j\leq d}x_j^j+\prod_{j\leq d}y_j^j=\prod_{j\leq d}z_j^j , \] with specific constraints $x_i\sim X^{a_i}$, $y_i\sim X^{b_i}, z_i\sim X^{c_i}$ on the size of the variables, for admissible values of $a_i,b_i,c_i$ (depending on $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$). We then bound the number of solutions to these Diophantine equations using four different methods. The first of these (Proposition~\ref{prop:FourierAnalysis}) uses Fourier analysis and Cauchy-Schwarz to estimate the number of solutions, leading to a bound that works well if two of the exponent vectors $(a_i)_i,(b_i)_i,(c_i)_i$ are somewhat ``correlated''. The second method (Proposition~\ref{prop:GeometryofNumbers}) uses the geometry of numbers and gives good bounds when one of $a_1,b_1,c_1$ is large. The remaining tools come from the determinant method of Heath-Brown (Proposition~\ref{prop:DeterminantMethod}) and uniform upper bounds for the number of solutions to Thue equations (Proposition~\ref{prop:ThueEquations}). For every choice of the exponents $a_i,b_i,c_i$ we shall need to take the minimum of these bounds, which leads to a rather intricate combinatorial optimisation problem. This is solved by showing that at least one of the four methods always gives a power-saving over Proposition~\ref{prop:ABCTrivialBound} when $\lambda$ is close to $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to counting solutions of monomial Diophantine equations, bound them by four methods, and solve the resulting optimisation problem.

nodes.name: Dyadic notation and [d]
nodes.statement: We shall use $x\sim X$ to denote $x\in [X,2X]$ and we put $[d]=\{1,\dots,d\}$.

nodes.name: Divisor function
nodes.statement: We denote by $\tau(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}1$ the divisor function.

nodes.name: Dyadic counting function S*
nodes.statement: Let $S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$ to be the number of $(a,b,c)\in \mathbb{N}^3$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ and \begin{align*} c\in [X/2,X],\quad a+b=c,\quad \rad(a)\sim X^{\alpha},\quad \rad(b)\sim X^{\beta},\quad \rad(c)\sim X^{\gamma}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: S* counts coprime triples with c in [X/2,X], a+b=c, and radicals of dyadic sizes X^alpha, X^beta, X^gamma.
nodes.label: def:Sstar

nodes.name: Reduction from N_lambda to S*
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} N_\lambda(X)\ll (\log X)^4 \max_{\substack{ \alpha,\beta,\gamma>0\\ \alpha+\beta+\gamma\leq \lambda}} S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: By pigeonhole, N_lambda(X) is at most (log X)^4 times the max of S* over alpha+beta+gamma <= lambda.
nodes.label: lem:NlambdatoSstar

nodes.name: Equation (2.1)
nodes.statement: N_\lambda(X)\ll (\log X)^4 \max_{\substack{ \alpha,\beta,\gamma>0\\ \alpha+\beta+\gamma\leq \lambda}} S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X).
nodes.label: eq:step1

nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{c}\in \mathbb{Z}^3$ and $\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d}$. we have \begin{equation} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) := \#\left\{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z})\in \mathbb{N}^{3d}\;:\; \begin{array}{l} x_i\sim X_i,\,y_i\sim Y_i,\,z_i\sim Z_i \\ c_1\prod_{j\leq d}x_j^j+c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j^j=c_3\prod_{j\leq d}z_j^j\\ \gcd(c_1\prod_{j\leq d}x_j,c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j , c_3\prod_{j\leq d}z_j)=1 \end{array} \right\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Factorisation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon\in (0,1/2)$, and let $2\leq n\leq X$ be an integer. Then there exists a factorisation \begin{align*} n=c\prod_{j\leq \frac{5}{2}\varepsilon^{-2}}x_j^{j}, \end{align*} for positive integers $x_j,c$ such that $c\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}$, the $x_j$ are pairwise coprime, and \begin{align*} X^{-\varepsilon}\prod_{j\leq \frac{5}{2}\varepsilon^{-2}}x_j \leq \rad(n) \leq X^{\varepsilon}\prod_{j\leq \frac{5}{2}\varepsilon^{-2}}x_j. \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $\varepsilon\in (0,1/2)$, and let $2\leq n\leq X$ be an integer.
nodes.statement_short: Every n <= X factors as c times prod x_j^j with c small, x_j pairwise coprime, and rad(n) close to prod x_j.
nodes.label: lem:DiophantineFactor

eq K$},\ y_j\prod_{m>M}y_m^{\lfloor m/Kfloor} & 	ext{for $j=K$}, \end{cases}\qquad	ext{and}\qquad c\,:=\prod_{m>M}y_m^{m-K\lfloor m/Kfloor}. \end{alignat*} All the $x_j$ are pairwise coprime, since the $y_j$ are pairwise coprime. Note that by definition $c\prod_{j\leq M}x_j^j=\prod_{m\geq 1}y_m^m=n\leq X$. In particular,  egin{align*} \prod_{m\geq M}y_m\leq \Big(\prod_{m\geq M}y_m^{m}\Big)^{1/M}\leq X^{1/M}. \end{align*} Then, since $m-K\lfloor m/Kfloor \le K$, it follows from the definition of $c$ that  egin{align*} c\leq \prod_{m\geq M}y_m^K\leq X^{K/M}\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}. \end{align*} Thus \[ ad(n)\leq ad(c)\prod_{j\leq M}ad(x_j)\leq X^{\varepsilon/2} \prod_{j\leq M} x_j. \] On the other hand, we have  egin{align*} x_K = y_K\prod_{m> M}y_m^{\lfloor m/Kfloor}\leq \Big(y_K^K\cdot\prod_{m> M}y_m^m\Big)^{1/K}\leq n^{1/K}\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}. \end{align*} Recalling that the $y_j$ are squarefree and pairwise coprime for $j
eq K$, gives the lower bound \[ ad(n)=\prod_{m\geq 1}y_m \geq \prod_{\substack{j\leq M\j
eq K}}x_j\geq X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq M}x_j, \] as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Group primes by exponent into y_j, fold high powers into x_K and c, then bound c and rad(n) on both sides.

nodes.name: Define y_j, x_j and c from the prime factorisation of n
nodes.statement: Fix $2\le n\le X$ and let $K=2\lceil \varepsilon^{-1}\rceil$, $M=\lfloor \frac{5}{2}\varepsilon^{-2}\rfloor$. Define \begin{align*} y_j:=\prod_{p^j\|n} p. \end{align*} For $j\leq M$, we set \begin{alignat*}{2} x_j:=\begin{cases}y_j & \text{for $j\neq K$},\\ y_j\prod_{m>M}y_m^{\lfloor m/K\rfloor} & \text{for $j=K$}, \end{cases}\qquad\text{and}\qquad c\,:=\prod_{m>M}y_m^{m-K\lfloor m/K\rfloor}. \end{alignat*}
nodes.statement_short: Define y_j, x_j and c from the prime factorisation of n.

nodes.name: The x_j are pairwise coprime
nodes.statement: All the $x_j$ are pairwise coprime, since the $y_j$ are pairwise coprime.
nodes.statement_short: The x_j are pairwise coprime.

nodes.name: Bound the product of y_m for m >= M
nodes.statement: Note that by definition $c\prod_{j\leq M}x_j^j=\prod_{m\geq 1}y_m^m=n\leq X$. In particular, \begin{align*} \prod_{m\geq M}y_m\leq \Big(\prod_{m\geq M}y_m^{m}\Big)^{1/M}\leq X^{1/M}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the product of y_m for m >= M.

nodes.name: Deduce c <= X^{eps/2}
nodes.statement: Then, since $m-K\lfloor m/K\rfloor \le K$, it follows from the definition of $c$ that \begin{align*} c\leq \prod_{m\geq M}y_m^K\leq X^{K/M}\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Deduce c <= X^{eps/2}.

nodes.name: Upper bound for rad(n)
nodes.statement: Thus \[ \rad(n)\leq \rad(c)\prod_{j\leq M}\rad(x_j)\leq X^{\varepsilon/2} \prod_{j\leq M} x_j. \]
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound for rad(n).

nodes.name: Bound x_K by X^{eps/2}
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we have \begin{align*} x_K = y_K\prod_{m> M}y_m^{\lfloor m/K\rfloor}\leq \Big(y_K^K\cdot\prod_{m> M}y_m^m\Big)^{1/K}\leq n^{1/K}\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound x_K by X^{eps/2}.

nodes.name: Lower bound for rad(n)
nodes.statement: Recalling that the $y_j$ are squarefree and pairwise coprime for $j\neq K$, gives the lower bound \[ \rad(n)=\prod_{m\geq 1}y_m \geq \prod_{\substack{j\leq M\\j\neq K}}x_j\geq X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq M}x_j, \] as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound for rad(n).

nodes.name: Diophantine reduction
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in (0,1]$ be fixed and let $X\geq 2$. For any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an integer $d=d(\varepsilon)\geq 1$ such that the following holds. There exist $X_1,\ldots, X_d,Y_1,\ldots, Y_d, Z_1,\ldots, Z_d\geq 1$ satisfying \begin{align} X^{\alpha-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon} \prod_{j=1}^{d}X_j\leq 2 X^{\alpha+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\beta-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon}\prod_{j=1}^{d}Y_j\leq 2 X^{\beta+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\gamma-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon}\prod_{j=1}^{d}Z_j\leq 2 X^{\gamma+\varepsilon} \end{align} and \begin{align} \prod_{j=1}^d X_j^j \leq X, \quad \prod_{j=1}^d Y_j^j\leq X,\quad X^{1-\varepsilon^2}\ll_{\varepsilon} \prod_{j=1}^d Z_j^j\leq X \end{align} and pairwise coprime integers $1\leq c_1,c_2,c_3\leq X^{\varepsilon}$, such that \begin{align*} S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X) \ll_{\varepsilon} X^{\varepsilon}B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: S* is bounded by X^eps times B_d for some dyadic sizes X_j,Y_j,Z_j and small coprime coefficients c.
nodes.label: prop:DiophantineReduction

nodes.name: Equation (2.4)
nodes.statement: X^{\alpha-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon} \prod_{j=1}^{d}X_j\leq 2 X^{\alpha+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\beta-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon}\prod_{j=1}^{d}Y_j\leq 2 X^{\beta+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\gamma-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon}\prod_{j=1}^{d}Z_j\leq 2 X^{\gamma+\varepsilon}
nodes.label: eq:xiyizi_1

nodes.name: Equation (2.5)
nodes.statement: \prod_{j=1}^d X_j^j \leq X, \quad \prod_{j=1}^d Y_j^j\leq X,\quad X^{1-\varepsilon^2}\ll_{\varepsilon} \prod_{j=1}^d Z_j^j\leq X
nodes.label: eq:xiyizi_2

nodes.name: Proof of Diophantine reduction
nodes.statement: We may assume that $X$ is large enough in terms of $\varepsilon$, since otherwise the claim is trivial. Let $(a,b,c)$ be a triple counted by $S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:DiophantineFactor} (with $\varepsilon^2/2$ in place of $\varepsilon$) to each of $a,b,c$ to obtain factorisations of the form \begin{align*} a=c_1\prod_{j\leq d}x_j^j,\quad b=c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j^j,\quad c=c_3\prod_{j\leq d}z_j^j, \end{align*} where $d=\lfloor 10\varepsilon^{-4}\rfloor$ and $1\leq c_1,c_2,c_3\leq X^{\varepsilon^2/4}$. Since $(a,b,c)$ is counted by $S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$, we have $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ and $a+b=c$, so $a,b,c$ are pairwise coprime. Hence, all the $3d+3$ numbers $x_i,y_i,z_i,c_1,c_2,c_3$ are pairwise coprime. Note also that by the properties of the factorisation given by Lemma~\ref{lem:DiophantineFactor}, we have \begin{align*} &X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}x_j\leq \rad(a)\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}x_j,\quad X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}y_j\leq \rad(b)\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}y_j,\\ &X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}z_j\leq \rad(c)\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}z_j. \end{align*} Since $\rad(a)\sim X^{\alpha},\rad(b)\sim X^{\beta},\rad(c)\sim X^{\gamma}$ for all triples under consideration, this implies \begin{align*} X^{\alpha-\varepsilon}\leq \prod_{j\leq d}x_j\leq X^{\alpha+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\beta-\varepsilon}\leq \prod_{j\leq d}y_j\leq X^{\beta+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\gamma-\varepsilon}\leq \prod_{j\leq d}z_j\leq X^{\gamma+\varepsilon}. \end{align*} By dyadic decomposition, we can now find some $X_i, Y_i,Z_i$ such that~\eqref{eq:xiyizi_1} and~\eqref{eq:xiyizi_2} hold, and such that \[ S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll_{\varepsilon} (\log X)^{3d} \sum_{\substack{\mathbf{c}\in \mathbb{N}^3\\ c_1,c_2,c_3 \leq X^{\varepsilon/4}}}B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}). \] Now the claim follows from the pigeonhole principle.
nodes.statement_short: Factor a, b, c by the factorisation lemma, then dyadic decomposition and pigeonhole.

nodes.name: Assume X large and apply the factorisation lemma to a, b, c
nodes.statement: We may assume that $X$ is large enough in terms of $\varepsilon$, since otherwise the claim is trivial. Let $(a,b,c)$ be a triple counted by $S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:DiophantineFactor} (with $\varepsilon^2/2$ in place of $\varepsilon$) to each of $a,b,c$ to obtain factorisations of the form \begin{align*} a=c_1\prod_{j\leq d}x_j^j,\quad b=c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j^j,\quad c=c_3\prod_{j\leq d}z_j^j, \end{align*} where $d=\lfloor 10\varepsilon^{-4}\rfloor$ and $1\leq c_1,c_2,c_3\leq X^{\varepsilon^2/4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume X large and apply the factorisation lemma to a, b, c.

nodes.name: All factors are pairwise coprime
nodes.statement: Since $(a,b,c)$ is counted by $S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$, we have $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ and $a+b=c$, so $a,b,c$ are pairwise coprime. Hence, all the $3d+3$ numbers $x_i,y_i,z_i,c_1,c_2,c_3$ are pairwise coprime.
nodes.statement_short: All factors are pairwise coprime.

nodes.name: Radicals are comparable to prod of x_j, y_j, z_j
nodes.statement: Note also that by the properties of the factorisation given by Lemma~\ref{lem:DiophantineFactor}, we have \begin{align*} &X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}x_j\leq \rad(a)\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}x_j,\quad X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}y_j\leq \rad(b)\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}y_j,\\ &X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}z_j\leq \rad(c)\leq X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leq d}z_j. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Radicals are comparable to prod of x_j, y_j, z_j.

nodes.name: Bound the products of x_j, y_j, z_j
nodes.statement: Since $\rad(a)\sim X^{\alpha},\rad(b)\sim X^{\beta},\rad(c)\sim X^{\gamma}$ for all triples under consideration, this implies \begin{align*} X^{\alpha-\varepsilon}\leq \prod_{j\leq d}x_j\leq X^{\alpha+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\beta-\varepsilon}\leq \prod_{j\leq d}y_j\leq X^{\beta+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\gamma-\varepsilon}\leq \prod_{j\leq d}z_j\leq X^{\gamma+\varepsilon}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the products of x_j, y_j, z_j.

nodes.name: Dyadic decomposition gives a sum of B_d
nodes.statement: By dyadic decomposition, we can now find some $X_i, Y_i,Z_i$ such that~\eqref{eq:xiyizi_1} and~\eqref{eq:xiyizi_2} hold, and such that \[ S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll_{\varepsilon} (\log X)^{3d} \sum_{\substack{\mathbf{c}\in \mathbb{N}^3\\ c_1,c_2,c_3 \leq X^{\varepsilon/4}}}B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}). \]
nodes.statement_short: Dyadic decomposition gives a sum of B_d.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole
nodes.statement: Now the claim follows from the pigeonhole principle.
nodes.statement_short: Pigeonhole.

nodes.name: Fourier analysis bound
nodes.statement: Let $d\geq 1$, $\varepsilon>0$ and $A\geq 1$ be fixed. Let \[ X_1,\ldots, X_d, Y_1,\ldots, Y_d,Z_1,\ldots, Z_d\geq 1 \] and put \begin{equation} \Delta =\max_{1\leq i\leq d}(X_i Y_i Z_i). \end{equation} Let $\mathbf{c}=(c_1,c_2,c_3)\in \mathbb{Z}^3$ satisfy $0<|c_1|,|c_2|,|c_3|\leq \Delta^A$. Then \begin{align*} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \ll \Delta^\varepsilon \frac{\prod_{j\leq d} \big(X_j Y_j Z_j(Y_j+Z_j)\big)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\max_{i>1}\prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}Z_j^{\frac{1}{2}}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Fourier analysis bound for B_d in terms of X_j Y_j Z_j (Y_j+Z_j), saving from Z_j with i | j.
nodes.label: prop:FourierAnalysis

nodes.name: Equation (3.1)
nodes.statement: \Delta =\max_{1\leq i\leq d}(X_i Y_i Z_i).
nodes.label: eq:Delta

nodes.name: Proof of Fourier analysis bound
nodes.statement:
By the orthogonality of characters, we have  egin{align*} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) &\leq \int_0^1 \sum_{x_j\sim X_j}\sum_{y_j\sim Y_i}\sum_{z_j\sim Z_j}e\Big(\alpha\Big(c_1\prod_{j\leq d}x_j^j+c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j^j-c_3\prod_{j\leq d}z_j^j\Big)\Big)\dd{\alpha} 
onumber\ &= \int_{0}^1 S_1(\alpha)S_2(\alpha)S_3(-\alpha)\, \dd \alpha, \end{align*} where  egin{align*} &S_1(\alpha)=\sum_{x_1\sim X_1,\ldots, x_d\sim X_d}e(\alpha c_1x_1x_2^2\cdots x_d^d),\quad S_2(\alpha)=\sum_{y_1\sim Y_1,\ldots, y_d\sim Y_d}e(\alpha c_2y_1y_2^2\cdots y_d^d),\ &S_3(\alpha)=\sum_{z_1\sim Z_1,\ldots, z_d\sim Z_d}e(\alpha c_3z_1z_2^2\cdots z_d^d). \end{align*} Then Cauchy-Schwarz gives  egin{align} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \leq \left(\int_{0}^1|S_1(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alphaight)^{ rac{1}{2}}\left(\int_{0}^1|S_2(\alpha)|^2|S_3(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alphaight)^{ rac{1}{2}} \ =: \sqrt{I_1\,I_2}. \end{align} By Parseval's identity and the divisor bound, we have  egin{align} egin{split} I_1 =\int_{0}^1|S_1(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alpha &= \sum_{x_j\sim X_j orall j}\# ig\{(x_1',\ldots, x_d')\colon x_j'\sim X_j\,\,  orall j,\, x_1x_2^2\cdots x_d^d=x_1'x_2'^2\cdots x_d'^d  ig\}\ & \ll \prod_{j\leq d} X_j^{1+\varepsilon}, \end{split} \end{align} for any $\eps>0$. Using Cauchy-Schwarz again, for any $i\le d$ we have  egin{align*} |S_3(\alpha)|^2 =  igg|\sum_{z_j\sim Z_j\, orall j\leq d}e(\alpha c_3z_1\cdots z_d^d) igg|^2 &\leq T(\alpha)\prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}Z_{j}, \end{align*} where \[ T(\alpha)= \sum_{z_j\sim Z_j\,  orall j
ot \equiv 0 mod i} igg|\sum_{z_j\sim Z_j\,  orall j\equiv 0 mod i}e(\alpha c_3z_1\cdots z_d^d) igg|^2. \] Let $ir$ be the largest multiple of $i$ in $[1,d]$. Then  egin{align} egin{split} I_2 & = \int_{0}^1|S_2(\alpha)|^2|S_3(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alpha \ & \le \ \prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}Z_{j}\cdot\int_{0}^1|S_2(\alpha)|^2\,T(\alpha)\, \d\alpha\ & \ = \prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}Z_{j} \cdot 	ilde N, \end{split} \end{align} where $	ilde N$ is the number of \[ (z_1,\ldots, z_d,z_i',\ldots, z_{ir}')\in \mathbb{N}^{d+r}, \quad (y_1,\ldots, y_d)\in \mathbb{N}^{d},\quad (y_1',\ldots, y_d')\in \mathbb{N}^d \] such that \[ y_j, y_j'\sim Y_j, \quad z_j \sim Z_j, \quad z_j'\sim Z_j \] for all $j\leq d$, and \[ c_3\left(\prod_{j\equiv 0 mod i}z_j^j-\prod_{j \equiv 0 mod i}z_j'^jight)\prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}z_{j}^j +c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j^j-c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j'^j=0. \] Let us write  egin{align} 	ilde N=	ilde{N}_1+	ilde{N}_2, \end{align} where $	ilde{N}_1$ is the contribution to $	ilde N$ from tuples with $\prod_{j\equiv 0 mod i}z_j^j= \prod_{j \equiv 0 mod i}z_j'^j$, and $	ilde{N}_2$ is the contribution of the complementary tuples. Then by the divisor bound we have  egin{align} 	ilde{N}_1= \#\Big\{ y_j, y_j'\sim Y_j,\,z_j \sim Z_j\, orall j\leq d\,:\, \prod_{j}y_j^j=\prod_{j}y_j'^j\Big\} \ \ll \ \prod_j Z_j Y_j^{1+\eps}, \end{align} for any $\eps>0$. In order to bound $	ilde{N}_2$, we first note that $a-b\mid a^i-b^i$ for any integers $a
eq b$ and $i\geq 1$. Thus for any integers $n
eq 0$ and $i\geq 2$,  egin{align*} \#\{(a,b)\in \mathbb{Z}^2:a^i-b^i=n\}|\leq 	au(|n|)\max_{d\mid n}\#\{b\in \mathbb{Z}:(b+d)^i-b^i=n\}\ll_{\varepsilon} |n|^{\varepsilon}. \end{align*} This follows from the divisor bound and the fact that $(x+d)^i-x^i-n$ is a polynomial of degree $i-1$. (Importantly, this argument fails when $i=1$, since then the polynomial $(x+n)^i-x^i-n$ is identically $0$.) Hence, on appealing to the divisor bound, we obtain  egin{align} egin{split} 	ilde{N}_2&\ll \prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^2\cdot \max_{0<|n|\leq \Delta^{A+k^2}}\#\left\{  egin{array}{l} (z_1,\ldots,z_d,z_i',\ldots, z_{ir}')\in \mathbb{N}^{d+r}: z_j \sim Z_j\,z_j' \sim Z_j'\,  orall j\ c_3(\prod_{j\equiv 0 mod i}z_j^j-\prod_{j\equiv 0 mod i}z_j'^j)\prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}z_{j}^j=n \end{array}ight\}\ &\ll \prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^2Z_j^{\eps/2}\cdot \max_{0<|n|\leq \Delta^{A+k^2}}\#\Big\{(a,b,c)\in \mathbb{N}^{3}:\,\, c(a^i-b^i)=n \Big\}\ &\ll \Delta^\eps\prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^{2}. \end{split} \end{align} Combining~\eqref{eq:I2},~\eqref{eq:N},~\eqref{eq:N1} and~\eqref{eq:N2}, we deduce that  egin{equation}  egin{split} I_2 &\ll \Delta^\eps \prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}Z_{j} \cdot igg(\prod_j Y_j Z_j + \prod_{j} Y_j^2  igg) \ &\ll \Delta^\eps \prod_{j\equiv 0 mod i}Z_j^{-1}\cdot \prod_{j}\Big(Y_j Z_j^{2} + Y_j^2Z_j\Big). \end{split}\end{equation} Plugging~\eqref{eq:prop3.1I1} and~\eqref{eq:prop3.1I2} back into~\eqref{eq:Bc123}, we conclude that  egin{align*} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \leq \sqrt{I_1\,I_2}\ll \Delta^\eps \prod_{j\equiv 0 mod i}Z_j^{- rac{1}{2}}\cdot \prod_{j}(X_j Y_j Z_j(Y_j+Z_j))^{ rac{1}{2}}, \end{align*} which is the desired bound.
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality and Cauchy-Schwarz split B_d into I_1 I_2; bound I_1 by Parseval and the divisor bound. I_2 is bounded by counting solutions with a^i-b^i dividing n.

nodes.name: Write B_d as an integral of exponential sums
nodes.statement: By the orthogonality of characters, we have \begin{align*} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) &\leq \int_0^1 \sum_{x_j\sim X_j}\sum_{y_j\sim Y_i}\sum_{z_j\sim Z_j}e\Big(\alpha\Big(c_1\prod_{j\leq d}x_j^j+c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j^j-c_3\prod_{j\leq d}z_j^j\Big)\Big)\dd{\alpha} \nonumber\\ &= \int_{0}^1 S_1(\alpha)S_2(\alpha)S_3(-\alpha)\, \dd \alpha, \end{align*} where \begin{align*} &S_1(\alpha)=\sum_{x_1\sim X_1,\ldots, x_d\sim X_d}e(\alpha c_1x_1x_2^2\cdots x_d^d),\quad S_2(\alpha)=\sum_{y_1\sim Y_1,\ldots, y_d\sim Y_d}e(\alpha c_2y_1y_2^2\cdots y_d^d),\\ &S_3(\alpha)=\sum_{z_1\sim Z_1,\ldots, z_d\sim Z_d}e(\alpha c_3z_1z_2^2\cdots z_d^d). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write B_d as an integral of exponential sums.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz: B_d <= sqrt(I_1 I_2)
nodes.statement: Then Cauchy-Schwarz gives \begin{align} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \leq \left(\int_{0}^1|S_1(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alpha\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\int_{0}^1|S_2(\alpha)|^2|S_3(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alpha\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \ =: \sqrt{I_1\,I_2}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz: B_d <= sqrt(I_1 I_2).

nodes.name: Bound I_1 by Parseval and the divisor bound
nodes.statement: By Parseval's identity and the divisor bound, we have \begin{align}\begin{split} I_1 =\int_{0}^1|S_1(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alpha &= \sum_{x_j\sim X_j\forall j}\#\big\{(x_1',\ldots, x_d')\colon x_j'\sim X_j\,\, \forall j,\, x_1x_2^2\cdots x_d^d=x_1'x_2'^2\cdots x_d'^d \big\}\\ & \ll \prod_{j\leq d} X_j^{1+\varepsilon}, \end{split} \end{align} for any $\eps>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound I_1 by Parseval and the divisor bound.

nodes.name: Bound |S_3|^2 by T(alpha)
nodes.statement: Using Cauchy-Schwarz again, for any $i\le d$ we have \begin{align*} |S_3(\alpha)|^2 = \bigg|\sum_{z_j\sim Z_j\,\forall j\leq d}e(\alpha c_3z_1\cdots z_d^d)\bigg|^2 &\leq T(\alpha)\prod_{j\not \equiv 0\bmod i}Z_{j}, \end{align*} where \[ T(\alpha)= \sum_{z_j\sim Z_j\, \forall j\not \equiv 0\bmod i}\bigg|\sum_{z_j\sim Z_j\, \forall j\equiv 0\bmod i}e(\alpha c_3z_1\cdots z_d^d)\bigg|^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound |S_3|^2 by T(alpha).

nodes.name: Bound I_2 by a counting problem N tilde
nodes.statement:
Let $ir$ be the largest multiple of $i$ in $[1,d]$. Then  egin{align} egin{split} I_2 & = \int_{0}^1|S_2(\alpha)|^2|S_3(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alpha \ & \le \ \prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}Z_{j}\cdot\int_{0}^1|S_2(\alpha)|^2\,T(\alpha)\, \d\alpha\ & \ = \prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}Z_{j} \cdot 	ilde N, \end{split} \end{align} where $	ilde N$ is the number of \[ (z_1,\ldots, z_d,z_i',\ldots, z_{ir}')\in \mathbb{N}^{d+r}, \quad (y_1,\ldots, y_d)\in \mathbb{N}^{d},\quad (y_1',\ldots, y_d')\in \mathbb{N}^d \] such that \[ y_j, y_j'\sim Y_j, \quad z_j \sim Z_j, \quad z_j'\sim Z_j \] for all $j\leq d$, and \[ c_3\left(\prod_{j\equiv 0 mod i}z_j^j-\prod_{j \equiv 0 mod i}z_j'^jight)\prod_{j
ot \equiv 0 mod i}z_{j}^j +c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j^j-c_2\prod_{j\leq d}y_j'^j=0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound I_2 by a counting problem N tilde.

nodes.name: Split N tilde into diagonal and off-diagonal parts
nodes.statement: Let us write \begin{align} \tilde N=\tilde{N}_1+\tilde{N}_2, \end{align} where $\tilde{N}_1$ is the contribution to $\tilde N$ from tuples with $\prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}z_j^j= \prod_{j \equiv 0\bmod i}z_j'^j$, and $\tilde{N}_2$ is the contribution of the complementary tuples.
nodes.statement_short: Split N tilde into diagonal and off-diagonal parts.

nodes.name: Bound the diagonal part
nodes.statement: Then by the divisor bound we have \begin{align} \tilde{N}_1= \#\Big\{ y_j, y_j'\sim Y_j,\,z_j \sim Z_j\,\forall j\leq d\,:\, \prod_{j}y_j^j=\prod_{j}y_j'^j\Big\} \ \ll \ \prod_j Z_j Y_j^{1+\eps}, \end{align} for any $\eps>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the diagonal part.

nodes.name: Count solutions of a^i - b^i = n via divisors
nodes.statement: In order to bound $\tilde{N}_2$, we first note that $a-b\mid a^i-b^i$ for any integers $a\neq b$ and $i\geq 1$. Thus for any integers $n\neq 0$ and $i\geq 2$, \begin{align*} \#\{(a,b)\in \mathbb{Z}^2:a^i-b^i=n\}|\leq \tau(|n|)\max_{d\mid n}\#\{b\in \mathbb{Z}:(b+d)^i-b^i=n\}\ll_{\varepsilon} |n|^{\varepsilon}. \end{align*} This follows from the divisor bound and the fact that $(x+d)^i-x^i-n$ is a polynomial of degree $i-1$. (Importantly, this argument fails when $i=1$, since then the polynomial $(x+n)^i-x^i-n$ is identically $0$.)
nodes.statement_short: Count solutions of a^i - b^i = n via divisors.

nodes.name: Bound the off-diagonal part
nodes.statement: Hence, on appealing to the divisor bound, we obtain \begin{align}\begin{split} \tilde{N}_2&\ll \prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^2\cdot \max_{0<|n|\leq \Delta^{A+k^2}}\#\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (z_1,\ldots,z_d,z_i',\ldots, z_{ir}')\in \mathbb{N}^{d+r}: z_j \sim Z_j\,z_j' \sim Z_j'\, \forall j\\ c_3(\prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}z_j^j-\prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}z_j'^j)\prod_{j\not \equiv 0\bmod i}z_{j}^j=n \end{array}\right\}\\ &\ll \prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^2Z_j^{\eps/2}\cdot \max_{0<|n|\leq \Delta^{A+k^2}}\#\Big\{(a,b,c)\in \mathbb{N}^{3}:\,\, c(a^i-b^i)=n \Big\}\\ &\ll \Delta^\eps\prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^{2}. \end{split} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the off-diagonal part.

nodes.name: Combine into a bound for I_2
nodes.statement: Combining~\eqref{eq:I2},~\eqref{eq:N},~\eqref{eq:N1} and~\eqref{eq:N2}, we deduce that \begin{equation} \begin{split} I_2 &\ll \Delta^\eps \prod_{j\not \equiv 0\bmod i}Z_{j} \cdot\bigg(\prod_j Y_j Z_j + \prod_{j} Y_j^2 \bigg) \\ &\ll \Delta^\eps \prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}Z_j^{-1}\cdot \prod_{j}\Big(Y_j Z_j^{2} + Y_j^2Z_j\Big). \end{split}\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Combine into a bound for I_2.

nodes.name: Plug the bounds for I_1 and I_2 into Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement: Plugging~\eqref{eq:prop3.1I1} and~\eqref{eq:prop3.1I2} back into~\eqref{eq:Bc123}, we conclude that \begin{align*} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \leq \sqrt{I_1\,I_2}\ll \Delta^\eps \prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}Z_j^{-\frac{1}{2}}\cdot \prod_{j}(X_j Y_j Z_j(Y_j+Z_j))^{\frac{1}{2}}, \end{align*} which is the desired bound.
nodes.statement_short: Plug the bounds for I_1 and I_2 into Cauchy-Schwarz.

nodes.name: Equation (3.2)
nodes.statement: B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \leq \left(\int_{0}^1|S_1(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alpha\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\int_{0}^1|S_2(\alpha)|^2|S_3(\alpha)|^2\, \d\alpha\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \ =: \sqrt{I_1\,I_2}.

nodes.name: Equation (3.3)

nodes.name: Equation (3.6)
nodes.statement: \tilde{N}_1= \#\Big\{ y_j, y_j'\sim Y_j,\,z_j \sim Z_j\,\forall j\leq d\,:\, \prod_{j}y_j^j=\prod_{j}y_j'^j\Big\} \ \ll \ \prod_j Z_j Y_j^{1+\eps},

nodes.name: Equation (3.7)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \tilde{N}_2&\ll \prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^2\cdot \max_{0<|n|\leq \Delta^{A+k^2}}\#\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (z_1,\ldots,z_d,z_i',\ldots, z_{ir}')\in \mathbb{N}^{d+r}: z_j \sim Z_j\,z_j' \sim Z_j'\, \forall j\\ c_3(\prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}z_j^j-\prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}z_j'^j)\prod_{j\not \equiv 0\bmod i}z_{j}^j=n \end{array}\right\}\\ &\ll \prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^2Z_j^{\eps/2}\cdot \max_{0<|n|\leq \Delta^{A+k^2}}\#\Big\{(a,b,c)\in \mathbb{N}^{3}:\,\, c(a^i-b^i)=n \Big\}\\ &\ll \Delta^\eps\prod_{j\leq d}Y_j^{2}. \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:N2

nodes.name: Equation (3.8)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} I_2 &\ll \Delta^\eps \prod_{j\not \equiv 0\bmod i}Z_{j} \cdot\bigg(\prod_j Y_j Z_j + \prod_{j} Y_j^2 \bigg) \\ &\ll \Delta^\eps \prod_{j\equiv 0\bmod i}Z_j^{-1}\cdot \prod_{j}\Big(Y_j Z_j^{2} + Y_j^2Z_j\Big). \end{split}

nodes.name: Heath-Brown lattice point bound
nodes.statement: Let $\gcd(a_1,a_2,a_3)=1$. Then for $X_1,X_2,X_3>1$, we have \begin{align*} \#\left((x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\Z^3 \;:\; \gcd(x_1,x_2,x_3)=1,\, |x_i| \le X_i ,\, a_1x_1+a_2x_2+a_3x_3=0\right) \ll \ 1 \ + \ & \frac{X_1X_2X_3}{\max_i\{|a_i|X_i\}}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Eisenstein irreducibility criterion for g(x)-y^r
nodes.statement: Let $r\geq 1$ and let $g\in \C[x]$ be a polynomial which has at least one root of multiplicity $1$. Then the polynomial $g(x)-y^r$ is absolutely irreducible.
assumptions: Let $r\geq 1$ and let $g\in \C[x]$ be a polynomial which has at least one root of multiplicity $1$.
nodes.label: lem:EisensteinCrit

nodes.name: Proof of Eisenstein irreducibility criterion
nodes.statement: We may assume a factorisation $g(x)=l_1(x)^{e_1}\dots l_t(x)^{e_t}$, with pairwise non-proportional linear polynomials $l_1,\dots,l_t\in \C[x]$ and exponents $e_1,\dots,e_t\in \N$ such that $e_1=1$. But ${\C}[x]$ is a unique factorisation domain and so we can apply Eisenstein's criterion with the prime $l_1$ in order to deduce that $g(x)-y^r$ is irreducible over $ {\C}[y]$. It then follows that $g(x)-y^r$ is irreducible over $ \C$, as claimed in the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Eisenstein's criterion with the simple linear factor l_1 as prime.

nodes.name: Factor g into linear factors with e_1=1
nodes.statement: We may assume a factorisation $g(x)=l_1(x)^{e_1}\dots l_t(x)^{e_t}$, with pairwise non-proportional linear polynomials $l_1,\dots,l_t\in \C[x]$ and exponents $e_1,\dots,e_t\in \N$ such that $e_1=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor g into linear factors with e_1=1.

nodes.name: Apply Eisenstein's criterion with prime l_1
nodes.statement: But ${\C}[x]$ is a unique factorisation domain and so we can apply Eisenstein's criterion with the prime $l_1$ in order to deduce that $g(x)-y^r$ is irreducible over $ {\C}[y]$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Eisenstein's criterion with prime l_1.

nodes.name: Conclude absolute irreducibility
nodes.statement: It then follows that $g(x)-y^r$ is irreducible over $ \C$, as claimed in the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude absolute irreducibility.

nodes.name: Exponents and coefficients p,q,r,a_1,a_2,a_3
nodes.statement: Let $p,q,r$ be positive integers and let $a_1,a_2,a_3\in \Z_{\neq 0}$.

nodes.name: Counting function N(X,Y,Z)
nodes.statement: We shall require a good upper bound for the counting function \[ N(X,Y,Z)= \#\left\{ (x,y,z)\in \Z_{\neq 0}^3: \begin{array}{l} |x|\leq X, ~|y|\leq Y,~|z|\leq Z\\ \gcd(x,y)=\gcd(x,z)=\gcd(y,z)=1 \\ a_1x^p+a_2 y^q+a_3 z^r=0 \end{array} \right\}, \] for given $X,Y,Z\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: N(X,Y,Z) counts pairwise coprime nonzero solutions of a1x^p+a2y^q+a3z^r=0 in a box.

nodes.name: Bombieri-Pila theorem
nodes.statement: Let $f(x)$ be a $C^\infty$ function on a closed subinterval of $[0,N]$, and suppose that$F (x, f ) = 0$, where $F(x, y) \in \R[x, y]$ is absolutely irreducible of degree $d \ge 2$. Suppose that $|f'(x)| \le 1$. Then \begin{align*} \#\{(x,f(x))\in \{1,\ldots,N\}^2 \} \ll_d (\log N)^{O(N)} N^{1/d} \end{align*}
assumptions: Let $f(x)$ be a $C^\infty$ function on a closed subinterval of $[0,N]$
suppose that$F (x, f ) = 0$, where $F(x, y) \in \R[x, y]$ is absolutely irreducible of degree $d \ge 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Integer points on the graph of a smooth algebraic function of degree d number about N^{1/d}.
nodes.label: thm:BombieriPilaforDet

nodes.name: Heath-Brown p-adic determinant method
nodes.statement: Let $F\in \Z[x_1 ,\ldots, x_n]$ be an absolutely irreducible polynomial of degree $d$, and let $\eps > 0$ and $B_1,\ldots,B_n \ge 1$ be given. Define \begin{align*} B = \max_{(e_1,\ldots,e_n)}\Big( \prod_{i\le n} B_i^{e_i} \Big) \end{align*} where the maximum is taken over all integer $n$-tuples $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ for which the corresponding monomial $x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ occurs in $F$ with non-zero coefficient. Then there exists $D = D(n,d,\eps)$ and an integer $k$ with \begin{align*} k \ll_{n,d,\eps} T^\eps (\log \|F\|)^{2n-3} \exp\Big((n-1)\Big(\frac{\prod_{i\le n}\log B_i}{\log B}\Big)^{1/(n-1)}\Big) \end{align*} satisfying the following: There are $k$ polynomials $F_1,\ldots,F_k\in \Z[x_1 ,\ldots, x_n]$ coprime to $F$, with $\deg F_i \le D$, such that every root of $F(x_1 ,\ldots, x_n)=0$ with $x_i \le B_i$ is also a root of $F_j(x_1 ,\ldots, x_n)=0$, for some $j\le k$.
nodes.statement_short: Integer roots of an absolutely irreducible F in a box lie on few auxiliary hypersurfaces of bounded degree.
nodes.label: thm:HeathBrownpadicDet

nodes.name: Quadratic forms estimate
nodes.statement: Given integers $n,a_1,a_2\neq0$, there are at most $O_{\eps,D}(|na_1a_2 X_1 X_2|^{\eps})$ many solutions $(x_1,x_2)\in\Z^2$ such that $|x_i|\le X_i$ and \begin{align*} n = a_1 x_1^2 + a_2 x_2^2. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Representations of n by a binary diagonal quadratic form in a box are O(|n a1 a2 X1 X2|^eps).
nodes.label: thm:QuadraticFormsEstimate

nodes.name: Proof of quadratic forms estimate
nodes.statement: Suppose $n=a_1x_1^2+a_2x_2^2$. Then $a_1n=a_1^2x_1^2+a_1a_2x_2^2$. Let $D$ be the squarefree part of $a_1a_2$. Then the number of solutions $(x_1,x_2)$ with $|x_i|\leq X_i$ to this equations is at most the number of solutions $(m_1,m_2)$ to $a_1n=m_1^2+Dm_2^2$ with $|m_i|\leq X_ia_1a_2$. For any such solution, we have $m_1+\sqrt{-D}m_2\mid a_1n$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-D})$. The claim follows from the divisor bound in quadratic fields, in Lemma \ref{lem:DivisorBoundQuadField}.
nodes.statement_short: Transform to m_1^2+Dm_2^2 = a_1 n and apply the divisor bound in Q(sqrt(-D)).

nodes.name: Multiply through by a_1
nodes.statement_short: Multiply through by a_1.

nodes.name: Reduce to the form m_1^2 + D m_2^2
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be the squarefree part of $a_1a_2$. Then the number of solutions $(x_1,x_2)$ with $|x_i|\leq X_i$ to this equations is at most the number of solutions $(m_1,m_2)$ to $a_1n=m_1^2+Dm_2^2$ with $|m_i|\leq X_ia_1a_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the form m_1^2 + D m_2^2.

nodes.name: Solutions give divisors of a_1 n in Q(sqrt(-D))
nodes.statement: For any such solution, we have $m_1+\sqrt{-D}m_2\mid a_1n$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-D})$.
nodes.statement_short: Solutions give divisors of a_1 n in Q(sqrt(-D)).

nodes.name: Apply the divisor bound in quadratic fields
nodes.statement: The claim follows from the divisor bound in quadratic fields, in Lemma \ref{lem:DivisorBoundQuadField}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the divisor bound in quadratic fields.

nodes.name: Divisor bound in imaginary quadratic fields
nodes.statement: Let $\eps>0$. Let $D\ge1$ be a squarefree integer, and set $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-D})$. Then for all $\alpha\in K$, the number of ideals dividing $(\alpha)$ in $K$ is $O(N_\alpha^\eps)$.
assumptions: Let $D\ge1$ be a squarefree integer, and set $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-D})$.
conclusions: for all $\alpha\in K$, the number of ideals dividing $(\alpha)$ in $K$ is $O(N_\alpha^\eps)$
nodes.label: lem:DivisorBoundQuadField

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the divisor bound in quadratic fields
nodes.statement: Mimics the proof over the integers using the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, but with ideals [See link in comment]
nodes.statement_short: Mimic the integer divisor bound using unique factorisation of ideals.

nodes.name: Bombieri-Schmidt bound for Thue equations
nodes.statement: Given integers $n,a_1,a_2\neq0$ and $p\ge3$, there are at most $O(p^{1+\omega(|n|)})$ many solutions $(x_1,x_2)\in\Z^2$ such that $|x_i|\le X_i$ and \begin{align*} n = a_1 x_1^p + a_2 x_2^p. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A Thue equation a1x1^p + a2x2^p = n has O(p^{1+omega(n)}) solutions.
nodes.label: thm:BombierSchmidtforThueEqs

nodes.name: Number of distinct prime factors
nodes.statement: Let $\omega(n)$ denote the number of distinct prime factors of an integer $n$.
nodes.label: def:omega

nodes.name: Upper bound for omega(n)
nodes.statement: For any $n\ge2$, we have $\omega(n) \ll \log(3n)/\log\log(3n)$.
nodes.label: lem:omegaUpperBound

nodes.name: Mixed determinant method bound
nodes.statement: Let $\eps>0$ and $D\geq 1$ and assume that $p,q,r\in [1,D]$ are integers. Then \[ N(X,Y,Z)\ll_{\ve,D} Z \min\left(X^{\frac{1}{q}}, Y^{\frac{1}{p}} \right) (XY)^\ve, \] where the implied constant only depends on $\ve$ and $D$. Furthermore, if $p=q\geq 2$, then we have \[ N(X,Y,Z)\ll_{\ve,D} Z (|a_1a_2a_3|XYZ)^\ve. \]
assumptions: Let $\eps>0$ and $D\geq 1$ and assume that $p,q,r\in [1,D]$ are integers.
Let $\eps>0$ and $D\geq 1$ and assume that $p,q,r\in [1,D]$ are integers.

nodes.statement_short: N(X,Y,Z) << Z min(X^{1/q}, Y^{1/p}) (XY)^eps, and << Z (|a1a2a3|XYZ)^eps when p=q>=2.
nodes.label: lem:MixedDetMethods

nodes.name: Proof of mixed determinant method bound
nodes.statement_short: Fix z; the resulting curve is absolutely irreducible, so Bombieri-Pila or Heath-Brown's Theorem 15 bounds the points.

nodes.name: Fix z
nodes.statement: We fix a choice of non-zero integer $z\in [-Z,Z]$, of which there are $O(Z)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix z.

nodes.name: Bombieri-Pila would bound points on the curve
nodes.statement: When $z$ is fixed, the resulting equation defines a curve in $\mathbb{A}^2$ and we can hope to apply work of Bombieri-Pila~\cite[Theorem~4]{bp}, which would show that the equation has $O_{\ve,D}(\max(X,Y)^{\frac{1}{\max(p,q)}+\ve})$ integer solutions in the region $|x|\leq X$ and $|y|\leq Y$, where the implied constant only depends on $\ve$ and $D$.
nodes.statement_short: Bombieri-Pila would bound points on the curve.

nodes.name: The curve is absolutely irreducible by the Eisenstein lemma
nodes.statement: This is valid only when the curve is absolutely irreducible, which we claim is true when $z\neq 0$. But, for fixed $z\in \Z_{\neq 0}$ the polynomial $a_2y^q+a_3z^r$ has non-zero discriminant as a polynomial in $y$. Hence the claim follows from Lemma~\ref{eis}.
nodes.statement_short: The curve is absolutely irreducible by the Eisenstein lemma.

nodes.name: Use Heath-Brown's Theorem 15 instead
nodes.statement: Rather than appealing to Bombieri-Pila, however, we can get a sharper bound by using work of Heath-Brown~\cite[Theorem 15]{cime}.
nodes.statement_short: Use Heath-Brown's Theorem 15 instead.

nodes.name: Resulting bound for fixed z
nodes.statement: For fixed $z\in \Z_{\neq 0}$ this gives the bound $O_{\ve,D}(\min(X^{\frac{1}{q}},Y^{\frac{1}{p}})(XY)^\ve)$ for the number of available $x,y$.
nodes.statement_short: Resulting bound for fixed z.

nodes.name: Mixed Thue methods bound
nodes.statement: Let $\eps>0$ and $D\geq 1$ and assume that $p=q,r\in [1,D]$ are integers. Then \[ N(X,Y,Z)\ll_{\ve,D} Z (|a_1a_2a_3|XYZ)^\ve. \] where the implied constant only depends on $\ve$ and $D$.
assumptions: Let $\eps>0$ and $D\geq 1$ and assume that $p=q,r\in [1,D]$ are integers.
nodes.label: lem:MixedThueMethods

nodes.name: Proof of mixed Thue methods bound
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $p=q\geq 2$. Then, for given $z\in \Z_{\neq 0}$, we are left with counting the number of integer solutions to the equation $N=a_1x^p+a_2y^p$, with $|x|,|y|\leq \max(X,Y)$, and where $N=-a_3z^r$. For $p=2$ this is a classical problem in quadratic forms. The bound $O_{\ve,D}((|a_1a_2N|XY)^\ve)$ follows from Heath-Brown~\cite[Theorem~3]{cubic}, for example. For $p\geq 3$ we obtain a Thue equation. According to work of Bombieri and Schmidt~\cite{bs}, there are at most $O(p^{1+\omega(|N|)})$ solutions, for an absolute implied constant. Using the bound $\omega(|N|)\ll \log(3|N|)/(\log \log(3|N|))$, this is $O_{\ve,D}((|a_3|Z)^\ve)$, which thereby completes the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Fix z; for p=2 use quadratic form bounds, for p>=3 Bombieri-Schmidt for Thue equations plus the omega bound.

nodes.name: Fix z and reduce to N = a1 x^p + a2 y^p
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $p=q\geq 2$. Then, for given $z\in \Z_{\neq 0}$, we are left with counting the number of integer solutions to the equation $N=a_1x^p+a_2y^p$, with $|x|,|y|\leq \max(X,Y)$, and where $N=-a_3z^r$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix z and reduce to N = a1 x^p + a2 y^p.

nodes.name: Case p=2: quadratic forms bound
nodes.statement: For $p=2$ this is a classical problem in quadratic forms. The bound $O_{\ve,D}((|a_1a_2N|XY)^\ve)$ follows from Heath-Brown~\cite[Theorem~3]{cubic}, for example.
nodes.statement_short: Case p=2: quadratic forms bound.

nodes.name: Case p>=3: Bombieri-Schmidt for Thue equations
nodes.statement: For $p\geq 3$ we obtain a Thue equation. According to work of Bombieri and Schmidt~\cite{bs}, there are at most $O(p^{1+\omega(|N|)})$ solutions, for an absolute implied constant.
nodes.statement_short: Case p>=3: Bombieri-Schmidt for Thue equations.

nodes.name: Bound omega(|N|) to conclude
nodes.statement: Using the bound $\omega(|N|)\ll \log(3|N|)/(\log \log(3|N|))$, this is $O_{\ve,D}((|a_3|Z)^\ve)$, which thereby completes the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Bound omega(|N|) to conclude.

nodes.name: Determinant method bound
nodes.statement: Let $d\geq 1$, and let \[ X_1,\ldots, X_d, Y_1,\ldots, Y_d,Z_1,\ldots, Z_d\geq 1. \] Let $\mathbf{c}\in (c_1,c_2,c_3)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\neq 0}^3$. Then for $\Delta$ as in~\eqref{eq:Delta}, we have \[ B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \ll \Delta^\ve \prod_{j\leq d} X_j Y_j Z_j \cdot \min_{p,q\geq 1}\left( (X_p Y_q)^{-1} \min\left( X_p^{\frac{1}{q}} , Y_q^{\frac{1}{p}}\right)\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Determinant method bound for B_d, saving via min(X_p^{1/q}, Y_q^{1/p}).
nodes.label: prop:DeterminantMethod

nodes.name: Proof of determinant method bound
nodes.statement: Let $(x_1,\ldots, x_d,y_1,\ldots, y_d,z_1,\ldots, z_d)$ be a tuple counted by $B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})$. For any integers $p,q\geq 1$, we fix all but $x_p$ and $y_q$ and apply the first part of Lemma~\ref{lem:MixedDetMethods}. This gives \[ B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \ll \Delta^\ve \prod_{\substack{j\leq d\\ j\neq p }} X_j \prod_{\substack{j\leq d\\ j\neq q }} Y_j \prod_{\substack{j\leq d }} Z_j \cdot \min\left( X_p^{\frac{1}{q}} , Y_q^{\frac{1}{p}}\right) , \] from which the statement of the lemma easily follows.
nodes.statement_short: Fix all variables except x_p and y_q and apply the first part of the mixed determinant lemma.

nodes.name: Fix all but x_p and y_q and apply the mixed determinant lemm
nodes.statement: Let $(x_1,\ldots, x_d,y_1,\ldots, y_d,z_1,\ldots, z_d)$ be a tuple counted by $B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})$. For any integers $p,q\geq 1$, we fix all but $x_p$ and $y_q$ and apply the first part of Lemma~\ref{lem:MixedDetMethods}.
nodes.statement_short: Fix all but x_p and y_q and apply the mixed determinant lemma.

nodes.name: Resulting bound gives the claim
nodes.statement: This gives \[ B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \ll \Delta^\ve \prod_{\substack{j\leq d\\ j\neq p }} X_j \prod_{\substack{j\leq d\\ j\neq q }} Y_j \prod_{\substack{j\leq d }} Z_j \cdot \min\left( X_p^{\frac{1}{q}} , Y_q^{\frac{1}{p}}\right) , \] from which the statement of the lemma easily follows.
nodes.statement_short: Resulting bound gives the claim.

nodes.name: Thue equation bound
nodes.statement: Let $d\geq 1$, and let \[ X_1,\ldots, X_d, Y_1,\ldots, Y_d,Z_1,\ldots, Z_d\geq 1. \] Let $\mathbf{c}\in (c_1,c_2,c_3)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\neq 0}^3$. Then \[ B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \ll \Delta^\ve \prod_{j\leq d} X_j Y_j Z_j \cdot \min_{p\geq 2} \prod_{\substack{j\leq d \\ p\mid j}} (X_j Y_j)^{-1}, \] where $\Delta$ is given by~\eqref{eq:Delta}.
nodes.statement_short: Thue equation bound for B_d, saving the X_j Y_j with p | j.
nodes.label: prop:ThueEquations

nodes.name: Proof of Thue equation bound
nodes.statement: Let $(x_1,\ldots, x_d,y_1,\ldots, y_d,z_1,\ldots, z_d)$ be a tuple counted by $B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})$. We collect together all indices which are multiples of $p$ for any integer $p\geq 2$. Applying the second part of Lemma~\ref{lem:MixedThueMethods} now gives \[ B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \ll \Delta^\ve \prod_{\substack{j\leq d\\ j\not\equiv 0 \bmod{p} }} X_j Y_j Z_j \prod_{\substack{j\leq d\\ j\equiv 0 \bmod{p} }} Z_j, \] from which the statement easily follows.
nodes.statement_short: Group indices divisible by p and apply the mixed Thue lemma.

nodes.name: Take a tuple and group indices divisible by p
nodes.statement: Let $(x_1,\ldots, x_d,y_1,\ldots, y_d,z_1,\ldots, z_d)$ be a tuple counted by $B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})$. We collect together all indices which are multiples of $p$ for any integer $p\geq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a tuple and group indices divisible by p.

nodes.name: Apply the mixed Thue lemma
nodes.statement: Applying the second part of Lemma~\ref{lem:MixedThueMethods} now gives \[ B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) \ll \Delta^\ve \prod_{\substack{j\leq d\\ j\not\equiv 0 \bmod{p} }} X_j Y_j Z_j \prod_{\substack{j\leq d\\ j\equiv 0 \bmod{p} }} Z_j, \] from which the statement easily follows.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the mixed Thue lemma.

nodes.name: Range of lambda and delta
nodes.statement: We now have everything in place to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:ABCExceptionalBound} for any \[ \lambda\in (0,1+\delta-\eps). \] and \[\delta\le 0.001-\varepsilon.\]
nodes.statement_short: Prove the main theorem for lambda < 1+delta-eps with delta <= 0.001-eps.

nodes.name: Equation (4.1)
nodes.statement: \alpha+\beta+\gamma\le \lambda < 1+\delta -\eps.
nodes.label: eq:goat

nodes.name: Trivial bound for S*
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0$, and let $\varepsilon>0$ be fixed. Then \[ S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll X^{0.66-\varepsilon^2/2}, \] unless $\min\{\alpha+\beta, \beta+\gamma,\gamma+\alpha\}\geq 0.66-\varepsilon^2$.
nodes.label: prop:TrivialBoundforSstar

nodes.name: Proof of trivial bound for S*
nodes.statement: This is an immediate consequence of~\eqref{eq:trivial} (with $\varepsilon^2/2$ in place of $\varepsilon$).
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the trivial bound for S.

nodes.name: Standing setting for bounding B_d
nodes.statement: In the light of Proposition~\ref{prop:DiophantineReduction} (with $\ve^2$ in place of $\ve$), we wish to bound $B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})$ for any pairwise coprime integers $1\leq |c_1|,|c_2|,|c_3|\leq X^{\varepsilon^2}$, any fixed $d\geq 1$, and any choice of $X_i,Y_i,Z_i\geq 1$, for $1\leq i\leq d$ that satisfies ~\eqref{eq:xiyizi_1} and~\eqref{eq:xiyizi_2}. Moreover, $ \alpha,\beta,\gamma $ satisfy~\eqref{eq:goat}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound B_d for small coprime c and dyadic sizes satisfying the reduction constraints, with alpha+beta+gamma <= lambda.

nodes.name: Exponents a_i, b_i, c_i
nodes.statement: Define $a_i,b_i,c_i\in \R_{\geq0}$ via \[ X_i=X^{a_i}, \quad Y_i=X^{b_i}, \quad Z_i=X^{c_i}, \] for $1\leq i\leq d$, and $a_i=b_i=c_i=0$ for $i>d$.
nodes.label: def:aibici

nodes.name: Constraints on a_i, b_i, c_i
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{i\leq d} ia_i \leq 1, \quad \sum_{i\leq d} ib_i \leq 1, \quad 1-\ve^2\leq \sum_{i\leq d} ic_i \leq 1. \end{equation}
conclusions: \sum_{i\leq d} ia_i \leq 1, \quad \sum_{i\leq d} ib_i \leq 1, \quad 1-\ve^2\leq \sum_{i\leq d} ic_i \leq 1.
nodes.label: lem:aibiciconstraints

nodes.name: Equation (4.2)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i\leq d} ia_i \leq 1, \quad \sum_{i\leq d} ib_i \leq 1, \quad 1-\ve^2\leq \sum_{i\leq d} ic_i \leq 1.
nodes.label: eq:oat1

nodes.name: Proof of constraints on a_i, b_i, c_i
nodes.statement: Follows from~\ref{prop:DiophantineReduction}
nodes.statement_short: Follows from the Diophantine reduction.

nodes.name: Trivial constraints on a_i, b_i, c_i
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \sum_{i\leq d} (a_i+b_i)\geq 0.66-\varepsilon^2,\quad \sum_{i\leq d} (a_i+c_i)\geq 0.66-\varepsilon^2,\quad \sum_{i\leq d} (b_i+c_i) \geq 0.66-\varepsilon^2 \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \sum_{i\leq d} (a_i+b_i+c_i) \leq 1+\delta-\eps. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pairwise sums of the exponent totals are at least 0.66-eps^2 and the total is at most 1+delta-eps.
nodes.label: lem:Trivialaibici

nodes.name: Equation (4.3)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i\leq d} (a_i+b_i)\geq 0.66-\varepsilon^2,\quad \sum_{i\leq d} (a_i+c_i)\geq 0.66-\varepsilon^2,\quad \sum_{i\leq d} (b_i+c_i) \geq 0.66-\varepsilon^2
nodes.label: eq:oat4

nodes.name: Equation (4.4)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i\leq d} (a_i+b_i+c_i) \leq 1+\delta-\eps.
nodes.label: eq:oat3

nodes.name: Proof of trivial constraints on a_i, b_i, c_i
nodes.statement: Follows from~\eqref{eq:goat} and Proposition~\ref{prop:TrivialBoundforSstar}.
nodes.statement_short: From the range of alpha+beta+gamma and the trivial bound for S*.

nodes.name: Exponent nu
nodes.statement: It will be convenient to henceforth define \begin{equation*} \nu=2\varepsilon^2+\frac{\log B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z})}{\log X}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: nu is 2eps^2 plus the exponent of B_d relative to X.
nodes.label: def:nu

nodes.name: Deduction of the main theorem from nu <= 0.66
nodes.statement: Our goal is now to show that $\nu\le 0.66$, since then~\eqref{eq:S*} is a direct consequence of Proposition~\ref{prop:DiophantineReduction}. This will then imply Theorem~\ref{thm:ABCExceptionalBound}, via~\eqref{eq:step1} and~\eqref{eq:S->S*}.
nodes.statement_short: Show nu <= 0.66; then the Diophantine reduction and the reduction to S* give the main theorem.

nodes.name: Range of the exponent sums
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} 0.32 - \delta \leq \sum_{i\leq d} a_i ,~ \sum_{i\leq d} b_i ,~ \sum_{i\leq d} c_i \leq 0.34 + \delta- \frac{1}{2}\ve, \end{equation}
also_stated_at: Before proceeding to the main tools that we shall use to estimate $\nu$, we first show that we may assume that \begin{equation*} 0.32 - \delta \leq \sum_{i\leq d} a_i ,~ \sum_{i\leq d} b_i ,~ \sum_{i\leq d} c_i \leq 0.34 + \delta- \frac{1}{2}\ve, \end{equation*} using the argument of Proposition~\ref{prop:TrivialBoundforSstar}.
conclusions: 0.32 - \delta \leq \sum_{i\leq d} a_i ,~ \sum_{i\leq d} b_i ,~ \sum_{i\leq d} c_i \leq 0.34 + \delta- \frac{1}{2}\ve,
nodes.statement_short: We may assume each of sum a_i, sum b_i, sum c_i lies in [0.32-delta, 0.34+delta-eps/2].
nodes.label: prop:Eqn4Point5

nodes.name: Equation (4.5)
nodes.statement: 0.32 - \delta \leq \sum_{i\leq d} a_i ,~ \sum_{i\leq d} b_i ,~ \sum_{i\leq d} c_i \leq 0.34 + \delta- \frac{1}{2}\ve,
nodes.label: eq:oat5

nodes.name: Proof of range of the exponent sums
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $\sum_{i\leq d} c_i> 0.34 + \delta-\varepsilon/2$. Then~\eqref{eq:oat3} implies that \[ \sum_{i\leq d} (a_i + b_i)< 0.66-\frac{1}{2}\eps, \] whence~\eqref{eq:trivial} yields $\nu< 0.66$. This shows that we may suppose that the upper bound in~\eqref{eq:oat5} holds. Suppose next that $\sum_{i\leq d} c_i< 0.32 - \delta$. Then, by the upper bound in~\eqref{eq:oat5}, we have \[ \sum_{i\leq d} (b_i + c_i)< 0.66-\frac{1}{2}\eps, \] which is again found to be satisfactory, via~\eqref{eq:trivial}.
nodes.statement_short: If a sum is too large or too small, a pairwise sum is below 0.66 and the trivial bound gives nu < 0.66.

nodes.name: Case: sum c_i too large; trivial bound applies
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that $\sum_{i\leq d} c_i> 0.34 + \delta-\varepsilon/2$. Then~\eqref{eq:oat3} implies that \[ \sum_{i\leq d} (a_i + b_i)< 0.66-\frac{1}{2}\eps, \] whence~\eqref{eq:trivial} yields $\nu< 0.66$. This shows that we may suppose that the upper bound in~\eqref{eq:oat5} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Case: sum c_i too large; trivial bound applies.

nodes.name: Case: sum c_i too small; trivial bound applies
nodes.statement: Suppose next that $\sum_{i\leq d} c_i< 0.32 - \delta$. Then, by the upper bound in~\eqref{eq:oat5}, we have \[ \sum_{i\leq d} (b_i + c_i)< 0.66-\frac{1}{2}\eps, \] which is again found to be satisfactory, via~\eqref{eq:trivial}.
nodes.statement_short: Case: sum c_i too small; trivial bound applies.

nodes.name: Fourier bound for nu
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \nu & < \frac{1}{2}\Big(1+\delta +\sum_{i\leq d} \max(a_i,b_i) - \max_{m>1}(a_m,b_m)\Big). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Fourier analysis bound recast as an upper bound for nu.

nodes.name: Proof of Fourier bound for nu
nodes.statement: It follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:FourierAnalysis} that \[ \nu \leq 3\varepsilon^2+ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\leq d}\Big(a_i+b_i+c_i +\max(a_i,b_i) - \max_{m>1}b_m\Big). \] Permuting variables, the claim now follows from~\eqref{eq:oat3}.
nodes.statement_short: Take logs in the Fourier analysis bound and use (4.4).

nodes.name: Standing assumptions for the completion
nodes.statement: Assuming that $\delta\leq 0.001$ and $\ve>0$ is sufficiently small, the remainder of this paper is devoted to a proof of the upper bound \[\nu \le 0.66, \] for any choice of parameters $a_i,b_i ,c_i$ satisfying the properties recorded in~\eqref{eq:oat1}-~\eqref{eq:oat5}. From this point onward, we will tacitly assume those properties hold.

If $M :=\max_{i\ge4}M_i > \frac{3}{4}(0.09)$, then using $\delta\leq 0.001$ and the Determinant bound (with variables permuted) yields \begin{align*} \nu \le 1 +\delta- a_3 - M + \min\left(\frac{M}{3}, \frac{a_3}{4}\right) \le 1+\delta - a_3 - \frac{2}{3}M &\le 1+\delta-0.32 - \frac{1}{2}(0.09) \le 0.636. \end{align*} This is satisfactory.

nodes.statement: In this case,~\eqref{eq:Thue} and~\eqref{eq:Case2Basic2} give \[ b_3,c_3 \le 0.34-a_3+\delta \le 0.34 - (0.32-4\delta_s-s_1-2\delta) +\delta= 0.02+4\delta_s+s_1+3\delta. \] In view of~\eqref{eq:robin3} and our assumption $4s_1+s_2<0.4$, we deduce that \begin{align*} b_3+c_3 \le 0.12+8\eps + 2s_1+6\delta < 0.32-\frac{s_2}{2}+6\delta+8\eps. \end{align*} Since $\delta\leq 0.001$, we have $b_3+c_3 \le 0.33-\frac{s_2}{2}-\frac{\delta}{2}$. Hence Subcase $\mathbf{2.2}$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bound b_3, c_3 via (4.12) and (4.20), giving b_3+c_3 small and reducing to Subcase 2.2.

nodes.name: Bound b_3, c_3 using (4.12) and (4.29)
nodes.statement: In this case,~\eqref{eq:Thue} and~\eqref{eq:Case2Basic2} give \[ b_3,c_3 \le 0.34-a_3+\delta \le 0.34 - (0.32-4\delta_s-s_1-2\delta) +\delta= 0.02+4\delta_s+s_1+3\delta. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound b_3, c_3 using (4.12) and (4.29).

nodes.name: Bound b_3+c_3
nodes.statement: In view of~\eqref{eq:robin3} and our assumption $4s_1+s_2<0.4$, we deduce that \begin{align*} b_3+c_3 \le 0.12+8\eps + 2s_1+6\delta < 0.32-\frac{s_2}{2}+6\delta+8\eps. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound b_3+c_3.

nodes.name: b_3+c_3 below the Subcase 2.2 threshold
nodes.statement: Since $\delta\leq 0.001$, we have $b_3+c_3 \le 0.33-\frac{s_2}{2}-\frac{\delta}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: b_3+c_3 below the Subcase 2.2 threshold.

nodes.name: Reduce to Subcase 2.2
nodes.statement: Hence Subcase $\mathbf{2.2}$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Subcase 2.2.

nodes.name: Subcase 2.5
nodes.statement: $\nu \leq 0.66$ in the case $s.2 < 0.3$ and $0.066\leq s_2\leq 0.204$.
nodes.label: lem:Subcase2.5

nodes.name: Proof of Subcase 2.5
nodes.statement: It follows from~\eqref{eq:robin3} and~\eqref{eq:Case2Basic2} that \[ a_3 \geq 0.32-4\delta_s-s_1 -2\delta \geq 0.28-4\eps-s_1 -2\delta. \] Thus $a_3>0.34-s_1-s_2 +\delta$, since $s_2\geq 0.066 \ge 0.062+4\eps +3\delta$ and $\delta\leq 0.001$. It now follows from~\eqref{eq:Geotau3} that we may assume $\tau_3=a_3 \geq 0.33 -\frac{s_2}{2}- \frac{\delta}{2}$. Thus~\eqref{eq:Thue} gives $b_3,c_3 \le 0.34-a_3 +\delta< 0.01 +\frac{s_2}{2}+ \frac{3\delta}{2}$, which in turn gives $b_3+c_3 < 0.02+s_2 +3\delta$. Since $s_2\leq 0.204$ and $\delta\leq 0.001$, we deduce that $b_3+c_3<0.33-\frac{s_2}{2}-\frac{\delta}{2}$. Hence Subcase $\mathbf{2.2}$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: The sub-sum criterion forces a_3 large, so b_3+c_3 is small, reducing to Subcase 2.2.

nodes.name: Lower bound for a_3
nodes.statement: It follows from~\eqref{eq:robin3} and~\eqref{eq:Case2Basic2} that \[ a_3 \geq 0.32-4\delta_s-s_1 -2\delta \geq 0.28-4\eps-s_1 -2\delta. \]
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound for a_3.

nodes.name: a_3 exceeds the criterion's lower end
nodes.statement: Thus $a_3>0.34-s_1-s_2 +\delta$, since $s_2\geq 0.066 \ge 0.062+4\eps +3\delta$ and $\delta\leq 0.001$.
nodes.statement_short: a_3 exceeds the criterion's lower end.

nodes.name: Sub-sum criterion forces a_3 large
nodes.statement: It now follows from~\eqref{eq:Geotau3} that we may assume $\tau_3=a_3 \geq 0.33 -\frac{s_2}{2}- \frac{\delta}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sub-sum criterion forces a_3 large.

nodes.name: Bound b_3+c_3
nodes.statement: Thus~\eqref{eq:Thue} gives $b_3,c_3 \le 0.34-a_3 +\delta< 0.01 +\frac{s_2}{2}+ \frac{3\delta}{2}$, which in turn gives $b_3+c_3 < 0.02+s_2 +3\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound b_3+c_3.

nodes.name: b_3+c_3 below the Subcase 2.2 threshold
nodes.statement: Since $s_2\leq 0.204$ and $\delta\leq 0.001$, we deduce that $b_3+c_3<0.33-\frac{s_2}{2}-\frac{\delta}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: b_3+c_3 below the Subcase 2.2 threshold.

nodes.name: Reduce to Subcase 2.2
nodes.statement: Hence Subcase $\mathbf{2.2}$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Subcase 2.2.

nodes.name: Proof of Subcase 2.6
nodes.statement_short: Use earlier subcases to confine s_1, s_2, a_3, b_3, then apply the Fourier bound to (a,b) and (e,c). Averaging the two bounds gives nu <= 0.658.

nodes.name: The two criterion intervals overlap, giving (4.30)
nodes.statement: In this case we note that the intervals in \eqref{eq:Geotau3} overlap, since $\delta\leq 0.001$. Hence for any $\tau_3$ belonging to the set \eqref{eq:taujdef}, we have \begin{equation} \tau_3\in \left(0.34-s_1-s_2+ \delta, \; 0.33-\frac{\delta}{2}\right) \Longrightarrow \nu < 0.66. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The two criterion intervals overlap, giving (4.30).

nodes.name: Subcases 2.3, 2.4 bound s_1 and s_2
nodes.statement: Furthermore, in the light of Subcases $\mathbf{S_3}$ and $\mathbf{S_4}$, we may assume that $4s_1+3s_2\leq 0.71$ and $4s_1+s_2\geq 0.4$. In particular, these imply that $s_1\leq \frac{0.71}{4}\leq 0.1775$ and $s_2 \leq \frac{1}{3}(0.71 - 4s_1) \leq \frac{1}{3}(0.71-0.4+s_2)$, so that $s_2\leq 0.155$.
nodes.statement_short: Subcases 2.3, 2.4 bound s_1 and s_2.

nodes.name: Subcases 2.5 and 2.1 give s_2 < 0.066 and a_3 < 0.32
nodes.statement: Then, on appealing to Subcase $\mathbf{S}_5$, we may assume that $s_2< 0.066$. Similarly, it follows from Subcase $\mathbf{S}_1$ that we may also assume $a_3<0.32$.
nodes.statement_short: Subcases 2.5 and 2.1 give s_2 < 0.066 and a_3 < 0.32.

nodes.name: Deduce a_3 small
nodes.statement: Thus \eqref{eq:tau3S6} and the bound $\delta\leq 0.001$ imply that we may assume $a_3< 0.34-s_1-s_2+ \delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce a_3 small.

nodes.name: b_3+c_3 small would contradict (4.21)
nodes.statement: If we also had $b_3+c_3<0.34-s_1-s_2+\delta$, then we would have $s_3 = a_3 + b_3 +c_3 < 0.68-2s_1-2s_2+2\delta$. Combining this with \eqref{eq:s3>s12}, we would then conclude that $$ 0.68-2s_1-2s_2+2\delta> s_3 \ge 1-4\delta_s-3s_1-2s_2, $$ which implies that $s_1>0.32-4\delta_s-2\delta$. Recalling \eqref{eq:robin3} and the inequalities $s_1\leq 0.1775 $ and $\delta\leq 0.001$, this is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: b_3+c_3 small would contradict (4.21).

nodes.name: So b_3+c_3 is large; confine a_3, b_3
nodes.statement: Hence we may assume that $b_3+c_3\ge 0.34-s_1-s_2+ \delta$, and by \eqref{eq:tau3S6}, we may assume $\tau_3=b_3+c_3\geq 0.33-\frac{\delta}{2}$, so $b_3>0.165-\frac{\delta}{4}> 0.164$. Thus we have $a_3,b_3\in [0.164, 0.341-s_1-s_2]$, since $\delta\leq 0.001$. In particular the interval is nontrivial, so $s_1+s_2\le 0.1775$.
nodes.statement_short: So b_3+c_3 is large; confine a_3, b_3.

nodes.name: Apply the Fourier bound to (a_i,b_i)
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Fourier bound to (a_i,b_i).

nodes.name: Lower-bound m_1
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:black1} we have $3a_1 + 2a_2 + a_3 \ge \frac{1}{3}-4\delta_a$, and similarly, $3b_1 + 2b_2 +b_3 \ge \frac{1}{3}-4\delta_b$. Thus $m_1 \ge \frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{3}-2M_2 - M_3-4\max(\delta_a,\delta_b))$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower-bound m_1.

nodes.name: Deduce (4.31)
nodes.statement_short: Deduce (4.31).

nodes.name: Repeat with (e_i,c_i)
nodes.statement: Next, if $a_2<b_2$, let $e_i := a_i$ for all $i\ge1$, otherwise let $e_i := b_i$ for all $i\ge1$. In particular, note $e_2 = \min(a_2,b_2)$ and $e_3 \ge \min(a_3,b_3)\ge c_3$. By a similar argument with $(a_i,b_i)_i$ replaced by $(e_i,c_i)_i$, we have \begin{align*} \nu &\le 0.784 + \frac{1}{3}\big(\max(e_2,c_2)-\max(e_3,c_3)\big) - \frac{1}{2}\min(e_3,c_3)\\ &\le 0.784 + \frac{1}{3}\big(\max(e_2,c_2)-e_3\big) - \frac{1}{2}c_3. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Repeat with (e_i,c_i).

nodes.name: Average the two bounds: nu <= 0.658
nodes.statement:
Averaging the bound with \eqref{eq:nuleqM2}, we obtain  egin{align} 
u &\le 0.784 +  rac{1}{6} ig(\max(a_2,b_2)+\max(e_2,c_2)-a_3-e_3 ig) -  rac{1}{4}(b_3+c_3) 
onumber\ &\le 0.784 +  rac{1}{6}s_2 -  rac{5}{12}(b_3+c_3) 
onumber\ &\le 0.784 +  rac{1}{6}(0.066) -  rac{5}{12}(0.33 - 	frac{\delta}{2}) \le 0.658. \end{align} Here we used $\max(a_2,b_2)+\max(e_2,c_2) = \max ig(a_2+b_2, \, \max(a_2,b_2) + c_2 ig) \le s_2$ and $a_3+e_3 \ge b_3+c_3 \ge 0.33 -  rac{\delta}{2}$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Average the two bounds: nu <= 0.658.

nodes.name: Equation (4.30)
nodes.statement: \tau_3\in \left(0.34-s_1-s_2+ \delta, \; 0.33-\frac{\delta}{2}\right) \Longrightarrow \nu < 0.66.
nodes.label: eq:tau3S6

nodes.name: Equation (4.31)
nodes.statement: \nu & \le 0.784 + \frac{1}{3}\big(\max(a_2,b_2)-\max(a_3,b_3)\big) - \frac{1}{2}\min(a_3,b_3) \nonumber\\ &\le 0.784 + \frac{1}{3}\big(\max(a_2,b_2)-a_3\big) - \frac{1}{2}b_3
nodes.label: eq:nuleqM2

nodes.statement: Immediate from Lemmas~\ref{lem:Case1} and~\ref{lem:Case2}.
